summary: Release-specific guidance for arx-kw 0.5.0: context-bound data-key wrapping, wrapping-key rotation, and detached-tag storage. Recipes use minimal features and OS-generated keys. Imported structured analysis based on the frozen published crate; no separate review is recorded. The guide covers these three tasks, not the entire API.

findings.title: Bind a data key to a stable application context
findings.guidance: For context-bound GX wrapping enable gx and envelope, import ArxKW, and use encrypt_envelope/decrypt_envelope. Preserve the exact context bytes: the envelope does not store them, and a changed context fails authentication. Contexts are limited to 4096 bytes. Envelopes add 24 bytes and never silently fall back to legacy blobs.

findings.title: Select only the required variant and envelope features
findings.guidance: Disable default features for a minimal dependency graph. gx,envelope provides context-bound GX; g alone provides raw detached wrapping. In 0.5.0 a variant alone no longer enables envelope methods/constants. HMAC and SHA-256 follow envelope; ChaCha and arrayref follow variants; only EX/GX enable XChaCha. zeroize, subtle, and thiserror remain mandatory. Rust 1.88 is the crate minimum.

findings.title: Keep owned keys and recovered plaintext in erasing guards
findings.guidance: Use SecretKey for owned wrapping keys and prefer decrypt_envelope or decrypt_secret for drop-time erasure. Raw decrypt and decrypt_blob return Vec<u8>; immediately guard recovered plaintext with Zeroizing when using them. Do not print secret material. Drop-time wiping cannot erase borrowed inputs or guarantee removal of copied keys, registers, swap, or crash dumps.

findings.title: Authenticate before rotating a wrapping key
findings.guidance: Open the existing envelope under the old wrapping key and context, then wrap the authenticated data key under the new wrapping key using the same context. Keep the intermediate plaintext guarded. Persist and verify the replacement before retiring the old key; production rotation also requires transactions, backups, and key identifiers.

findings.title: Use dedicated keys with raw detached storage
findings.guidance: G accepts a 32-byte wrapping key and at most 64 plaintext bytes. encrypt returns ciphertext and a separate 16-byte AuthTag. Retain both, reject every decryption error, and use a dedicated key for this protocol: the raw format has no version, variant, or application context.

findings.title: Use deterministic wrapping for high-entropy key material
findings.guidance: Generate keys with a cryptographically secure random source. Deterministic wrapping reveals repeated inputs within a key and context; it is not general-purpose encryption for passwords or predictable messages. E/G accept up to 64 bytes; EX/GX up to one MiB. Applications must provide replay/rollback protection and key lifecycle management. This crate has no established independent cryptographic audit.

recipes.title: Wrap a data key for a tenant
recipes.description: Generate a data key and wrapping key from OS randomness; wrap with GX and verify recovery and wrong-context rejection. The example does not persist wrapping keys.

recipes.title: Rotate a wrapping key
recipes.description: Authenticate an existing envelope, rewrap under a new wrapping key, and verify that the data key is unchanged and the old key is rejected. Durable storage and transactional rotation remain application responsibilities.

recipes.title: Store ciphertext and tag separately
recipes.description: Use raw G wrapping with a dedicated protocol key, guard recovered plaintext, and verify rejection of a modified tag.
